analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates for companies paying their CEO more than 50 times their median worker.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2025 with 5 Senate cosponsors, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the corporate tax rate above the standard 21% for large companies whose CEO (or highest-paid employee) earns more than 50 times what their median worker earns. The surcharge climbs with the gap: 0.5 percentage points for ratios over 50-to-1, up to 5 points for ratios over 500-to-1. It uses a five-year average of the pay-ratio figures public companies already disclose, and it extends the requirement to large private companies with at least $100 million in annual revenue, while exempting smaller private businesses. It also directs Treasury to write rules preventing companies from gaming the ratio by replacing employees with contractors.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large companies with extreme pay gaps would gain the most if the tax creates pressure to raise median wages or trim executive pay. The federal government would also collect additional corporate tax revenue. Companies that keep pay ratios modest would face no increase.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at companies with big pay gaps

how_it_helps.text: Adds a surcharge on top of the 21% corporate rate, from 0.5 percentage points (pay ratio over 50-to-1) up to 5 percentage points (over 500-to-1), giving large companies a direct tax reason to close the gap between executive and typical worker pay.

Uses the pay-ratio disclosures public companies already make to the SEC, averaged over five years, so companies cannot dodge the surcharge with a single favorable year, and it applies to the highest-paid employee, not just the CEO, when that person earns more.

Covers large private corporations with average annual gross receipts of at least $100 million by requiring them to calculate and report a pay ratio under Treasury regulations, closing the most obvious route around the rule for big privately held firms.

Directs the Treasury Secretary to write regulations preventing manipulation of the ratio, including shifting work from employees to contractors, the workaround economists most expect companies to try.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations with pay ratios above 50-to-1 would pay higher federal taxes, a cost borne by their shareholders through lower returns. Companies could instead avoid the tax by raising median pay or reducing executive compensation. Consumers could see some of the cost passed through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large companies with extreme pay ratios

drawbacks.text: The surcharge may simply be absorbed as a cost of doing business: a company earning billions may find a 5-point rate increase cheaper than narrowing a 500-to-1 pay gap, leaving workers no better off and shareholders footing the bill.

The bill creates strong incentives to restructure pay and workforces, and although it directs Treasury to police contractor substitutions and other avoidance schemes, enforcement of such rules is notoriously difficult.

Businesses could pass some of the higher tax to consumers through prices, and the penalty scales on a formula that may not track genuine worker hardship, for example penalizing a company for a highly paid CEO even when its median workers earn well.
Private companies under $100 million in gross receipts are exempt, so similarly structured businesses face different treatment based only on their size.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but indirect: the bill does not mandate any wage change, it just taxes extreme pay gaps and hopes companies respond by narrowing them rather than paying the tax. The cost falls on shareholders of high-pay-ratio corporations, which is a defensible target, but the design leaves open the possibility that firms simply absorb the surcharge or engineer around it. As a statement of priorities it is clear; as an economic tool, its effectiveness depends heavily on regulations that do not yet exist.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice on the Senate floor, and sent to the Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the Tax Excessive CEO Pay Act of 2025 on September 16, 2025, joined by Senators Warren, Van Hollen, Markey, and Welch.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, and no further action appears in the record.
The bill has 5 cosponsors, all Democrats in a Senate where 60 votes are typically needed to advance most legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, large corporations with extreme CEO-to-worker pay ratios are better off: they face no added tax and no new reporting requirement. The status quo of wide executive pay gaps continues.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on September 16, 2025.

for.name: Chris Van Hollen, Ed Markey, and Peter Welch

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup since its referral; no Finance Committee action appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 5 cosponsors are Democrats or left-leaning independents in a Senate with 45 Democrats, 2 independents, and 55 Republicans, and no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.industry: Large public corporations with high CEO pay ratios
industries.note: These companies would pay 0.5 to 5 percentage points more in federal corporate tax until they shrink the gap between executive and median worker pay. Their interest in avoiding the tax runs directly against the bill's goal of narrowing pay inequality.

industries.industry: Large privately held companies (over $100 million gross receipts)
industries.note: They would face a new pay-ratio calculation and reporting requirement, and the tax itself if their ratios exceed 50-to-1. Workers at these firms would benefit if the tax pushes pay upward.
Private companies under $100 million in average annual gross receipts are exempt from the pay-ratio calculation and the tax increase.
Requiring large private firms to compute and report pay ratios would create new demand for compensation analysis and compliance services.

analysis.trajectory: With only 5 cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action in the months since referral, the bill is very likely to die in the Senate Finance Committee when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, unless a companion bill or political moment revives it. Its realistic near-term role is as a statement of principle that could be reintroduced in the next Congress.
